symbols.name: EventMap
symbols.description: Native events dispatched through `Events.on`. Each property is the exact callback argument tuple for that event.

properties.name: playerReady
properties.description:
Dispatched once per session, when the local player can play: the session is established and the game has taken its own loading screen down. The game raises that moment itself -- it is its own gameplay-start signal, not a guess from timing.

Resources are running long before this, so it is not the moment a resource may start listening; it is the moment the player is looking at the world. Put what the player should see on arrival here -- a welcome, a first page -- rather than in `resourceStart`, which runs behind the loading screen. The server raises its own `playerReady` for this player right after.

properties.name: progressionXpGained
properties.description: Dispatched when the local player's XP on a track went up: after the server granted a gain and the game applied it, with its own multipliers. `xp` is what landed, in the game's own units.

properties.name: progressionLevelUp
properties.description: Dispatched when a track of the local player's reaches a new level. `perkPoints` is what that track's tree now has unspent.

properties.name: progressionPerkAdded
properties.description: Dispatched when the local player gained a perk: learnt on the perk screen and granted by the server, given by a server resource, or granted by the game on its own.

properties.name: progressionPerkRemoved
properties.description: Dispatched when the local player lost a perk.

properties.name: progressionPerkRefused
properties.description: Dispatched when the server turned down a perk the local player confirmed on the perk screen. The game's own screen says nothing when that happens, so this is where a resource tells the player why.

properties.name: monologueSuppressed
properties.description: Dispatched when a monologue line of the local character -- a photo-mode comment, the sharpening remark -- was kept silent and unsubtitled. `text` is localized; `textKey` is its localization key. Not raised while `Hud.setMonologueEnabled(true)` has released it. Handler promises are not awaited.

properties.name: storyCutsceneSuppressed
properties.description: Dispatched when a quest asked to play a story cutscene and multiplayer kept it from playing, so the player stays in control and the world clock runs on. `cutscene` is its name in the game's cutscene table. Not raised while `Hud.setStoryCutscenesEnabled(true)` has released them. Handler promises are not awaited.

properties.name: questTrackingChanged
properties.description: Dispatched when this player starts or stops following a server quest in the game's journal, whichever way it happened: the track button, the game auto-tracking a quest that turns active, or the untrack that follows finishing or failing one. Local to this machine and raised before the server is told; the server raises its own `questTrackingChanged` when the report arrives. Repeats are filtered, so it only fires on an actual change. Handler promises are not awaited.

properties.name: doorInteract
properties.description:
Dispatched on this machine when the local player uses a door, before anything happens: the door has not moved, the body has not started, and the server has not been told. `action` is `open`, `close`, `unlock` or `lockpick`, as server-side `doorInteract` has it; a key turned in the same use as the push arrives as `unlock` and then `open`, and refusing the `unlock` refuses the use without asking about the `open`. `keySide` says whether the player stands on the side with the keyhole.

Return false to refuse it: the use does nothing, with no round trip and nothing to put back. Every handler runs whatever an earlier one returned, and an async handler cannot refuse. A door the server made unusable (`door.usable` there) offers no prompt and never gets here.

It is this machine's own rule. The server's `doorInteract` still decides what it is told, so a refusal that has to hold against a modified client belongs there as well.

properties.name: vendorOpened
properties.description: Dispatched when the game's trade screen actually comes up on this machine for a server vendor -- not when the server asked for it, which can take a few frames or fail. `npc` is the network ID of the NPC keeping the shop, or null when nobody does. Every `vendorOpened` is followed by exactly one `vendorClosed`.

properties.name: vendorClosed
properties.description: Dispatched when a trade screen that `vendorOpened` announced goes away: the player closed it, the server closed it, the server opened another vendor over it, the level changed under it, or the connection ended. A screen that never came up raises neither event. The server raises its own `vendorClosed` for the session.

properties.name: poiDiscovered
properties.description: Dispatched when a point of interest becomes discovered at this machine: silently while the server's `reveal_map` is on, as the game's own discovery when it is off, and for each one `WorldMap.discover` marks. Handler promises are not awaited. A position merely made known emits nothing.

properties.name: locationDiscovered
properties.description: Dispatched when a location -- a town, a district -- becomes discovered at this machine through the game's own discovery, which only happens while the server's `reveal_map` is off. `WorldMap.discover` does not raise it. Handler promises are not awaited.

properties.name: weaponHit
properties.description: Dispatched on this machine when the local player's swing meets something solid that is not a body: a tree, a wall, a rock, a prop, the ground. Once per thing per attack, at the first contact, as the game itself counts it; a blade that rests against a wall is not reported again. `hit` is named as a trace names it, with `distance` measured from the player's feet. Fists and kicks are not reported, and neither is a blow on a player, an NPC or an animal, which `playerHit` and the damage events cover. The server hears of it as `playerWeaponHit`.

properties.name: mapOpened
properties.description: Dispatched when the map screen comes up at this machine.

properties.name: mapClosed
properties.description: Dispatched when the map screen goes away.

properties.name: mapWaypointSet
properties.description: Dispatched when the player drops their own marker on the map, or moves the one already down -- `moved` separates the two, because the game uses one action for both. The position is world-space metres. Maps reuse one coordinate range, which is why `mapId` travels with it.

properties.name: mapWaypointCleared
properties.description: Dispatched when the player takes their marker off the map, including through `WorldMap.clearWaypoint`. It carries where the marker was, since afterwards nothing says.

properties.name: noclipChanged
properties.description:
Dispatched when the flight starts and when it ends, on this machine only. Handler promises are not awaited.

`reason` is `script` on the way in. On the way out it is `script` for a resource ending it, `mapEditor` for the map editor taking the one camera, `viewLost` for the level going away underneath the camera's anchor, and `sessionOver` for the session ending.

properties.name: bookOpened
properties.description: Dispatched when a book `Book.open` asked for is in the player's hands and showing its first page, on this machine only.

properties.name: bookClosed
properties.description: Dispatched when a book leaves the player's hands, on this machine only. `reason` is `player` for the player's own exit (or the game ending the reading itself), `script` for `Book.close`, `failed` for a book that never reached the hands, and `sessionOver` for the session ending. Handler promises are not awaited, and a handler may open the next book straight away.

properties.name: followStarted
properties.description: The local native follow action has entered. A successful start request may still fail before this event.

properties.name: followStopped
properties.description: A queued or active scripted follow ended on this client.

properties.name: characterCreatorClosed
properties.description: Dispatched once for every creator, on this machine only, whatever ended it. `appearance` is the look the player accepted, and null for every other ending. `reason` is `accepted`, `cancelled` for the player backing out, `closed` for `CharacterCreator.close`, `replaced` for another `CharacterCreator.open`, `unavailable` when the stage could not be put up, and `interrupted` when the session or the body went away under it. Nothing is put on the body: send the look wherever it should go -- `Events.emitServer`, then `player.setAppearance` on the server -- or open the next creator straight from the handler.

properties.name: actionHintsChanged
properties.description: Dispatched when what the HUD's hints say changes: one appears or goes, changes its text, is greyed out, or a hold ring moves. `ActionHint.shown()` reads the new set. Handler promises are not awaited.

properties.name: resourceStart
properties.description: Dispatched after a resource entry point has run and immediately before the resource becomes running.

properties.name: resourceStop
properties.description: Dispatched while a resource is stopping, before its stop callback, timers, exports and event handlers are cleaned up.

properties.name: entityStateChange
properties.description: Dispatched when one key of an entity's state changes: on the server when a script writes it, on a client when the write arrives. `value` is undefined when the key was removed and `previous` is undefined when it held nothing before, so a stored null stays distinguishable from an absent key. The entity is whatever the game's WrapScriptEntity answers, and the base Entity handle by default.

type.name: [entity: Entity, key: string, value: any, previous: any]

properties.name: browserCreated
properties.description: Dispatched once per view, before any navigation, to the resource that created it.

properties.name: browserLoadingStart
properties.description: Dispatched when any frame of an owned view begins loading.

properties.name: browserDocumentReady
properties.description: Dispatched when an owned view's main document is ready; the earliest point at which the page can receive Web.emit.

properties.name: browserLoadingFailed
properties.description: Dispatched when a frame of an owned view fails to load.

properties.name: browserNavigate
properties.description: Dispatched for every navigation an owned view is asked to perform, refused or not.

properties.name: browserPopup
properties.description: Dispatched when an owned view blocks a popup; windowless views cannot host one, so handle the URL yourself.

properties.name: browserCursorChange
properties.description: Dispatched when an owned view's requested cursor shape changes.

properties.name: browserTooltip
properties.description: Dispatched when an owned view requests a tooltip; windowless rendering draws none, so the script must.

properties.name: browserInputFocusChange
properties.description: Dispatched when focus enters or leaves an editable element of an owned view; use it to stop routing keys to the game.

properties.name: browserResourceBlocked
properties.description: Dispatched when an owned view rejects a navigation or a page event from outside its locked origin.

properties.name: browserConsoleMessage
properties.description: Dispatched for console output of an owned view; the framework logs these regardless.

properties.name: browserOriginChange
properties.description: Dispatched on view creation and whenever Web.loadURL re-locks an owned view to a different origin.

symbols.name: Appearance
symbols.description:
How a player's body looks: four of the game's own character-component names, and the gender whose catalog they come from.

A part left out, or set to an empty string, means "leave that one alone" -- the body keeps whatever it would have had. An appearance with every part empty is the default body, which is what everyone wears until something chooses otherwise.

properties.name: gender
properties.description: Which half of the game's character-component tree the four names come from. Not one of the four: a body's gender comes from its soul, and a name from one tree means nothing under the other, so this travels with them and is applied first.

properties.name: body
properties.description: The skin: complexion and build. One of `Appearances.options("body", gender)`, or empty.

properties.name: head
properties.description: The face. One of `Appearances.options("head", gender)`, or empty.

properties.name: hair
properties.description: The hairstyle, including its colour -- the game ships each style recoloured rather than colouring one. One of `Appearances.options("hair", gender)`, or empty.

properties.name: beard
properties.description:
The beard. Male only -- the female tree has none -- and one of `Appearances.beards(head)`, or empty.

Not every beard goes with every face: they are modelled per head, and a body asked for a pair that was never modelled refuses the whole appearance rather than quietly losing the beard.

symbols.name: AppearanceOption
symbols.description: One entry of the game's character-component tree: something a body can be given for one part.

properties.name: name
properties.description: What to put in the part. This is the game's own node name.

properties.name: part
properties.description: Which part it fills.

properties.name: gender
properties.description: Which tree it came out of. An option is only valid on a body of the same gender.

properties.name: group
properties.description: The option this one is a variation of, or null when it stands on its own. The game ships a hairstyle once per colour, all derived from the same style node, so grouping by this is what turns 262 hairstyles into a list somebody can read.

symbols.description: A KCDC player this client can see, and the body they occupy.

constructor.name: constructor
constructor.description: Creates a script wrapper for a player this client already knows about; it neither connects nor spawns anyone.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: Network entity identifier.

functions.name: toString
functions.description: Formats this player handle for logging and debugging.

returns.description: The player's network entity ID, nickname, and whether they are the local player.

functions.name: getStat
functions.description: Reads the latest reported stat in native units. Returns zero when no valid body snapshot exists; check player.ready to distinguish that from a real zero. Throws for an unknown stat or invalid arguments.

parameters.name: stat
parameters.description: A PlayerStat value.

functions.name: getDerivedStat
functions.description: Reads a computed stat from the latest body snapshot. Bleeding, Sleeping, Consciousness, Drunkenness and Poisoning follow the body as it changes; the others are sampled about every 250 ms to a hundredth of a native unit, then replicated. Values use native units and can be negative; they are not universally percentages. Returns zero without a valid snapshot. Throws for an unknown stat or invalid arguments. These readings do not override another player's native calculations.

parameters.name: stat
parameters.description: A DerivedPlayerStat value.

functions.name: getTrack
functions.description: Where the local player stands on one track: level, XP towards the next one, and unspent perk points. Only the local player carries XP and points; for anyone else this is null.

parameters.name: track
parameters.description: A track name, from `Progression.tracks()`.

returns.description: The progress, or null for any other player. Throws for a track name the tables do not carry.

functions.name: hasPerk
functions.description: Whether the player owns a perk.

parameters.name: perk
parameters.description: A perk's name or GUID.

returns.description: True when they do; false for a perk they do not own, or a name the tables do not carry.

functions.name: setTargetable
functions.description: Keeps another player's body out of this machine's combat lock-on and opponent picker, or lets it back in -- for someone lying wounded, say. Only this client's picker is affected, so a resource that wants it everywhere tells every client. It does not stop a swing that lands anyway; damage is the server's to refuse. Lasts until changed or the session ends. Throws unless `targetable` is a boolean.

parameters.name: targetable
parameters.description: False to keep this player's body out of the local lock-on, true to let it back.

properties.name: nickname
properties.description: The name this player connected under, or an empty string once their body is gone.

properties.name: playerIndex
properties.description: Connection slot this player holds, or 65535 when unassigned. Stable for the length of the session and reused afterwards.

properties.name: appearance
properties.description:
What this player's body looks like, as their own client last published it. Every part is empty until something chooses one, which is the default body -- and why everyone looks the same until a resource says otherwise.

Read back rather than assumed after `setAppearance`: the owning client is authoritative for its own body, so a new look appears here once they have actually put it on.

properties.name: disguise
properties.description: The prop-catalog mesh this player's body is drawn as, by its `objects/...cgf` path, or null while they look like themselves. Published by their own client, so it follows `setDisguise` once they have actually put it on.

properties.name: visible
properties.description: Whether this player's body is drawn at all -- itself, what it wears and what it carries. True for everybody until something hides them. Published by their own client, so it follows `setVisible` once they have actually stopped drawing. A hidden player is only invisible: they still stand where they stand, still collide, can still be hit, and NPCs still see them.

properties.name: ready
properties.description: Whether this player's body has both a pose and a soul, which is what everyone else waits for before spawning a puppet for them. False for the first moments of a connection.

properties.name: alive
properties.description: Whether this player has health left. False also while no soul has been published.

properties.name: canAct
properties.description: Whether the body can be driven at all: alive, conscious and not asleep.

functions.name: addScreenEffect
functions.description:
Puts a full-screen effect on this player's own picture -- a colour grade, a blur, ghosting or the game's blood overlay, for intoxication, injury, poison, dreams or a place that should feel wrong -- owned by the calling resource. These are the game's own post-processing passes, driven with the parameters this build actually reads; they are not part of the HUD and showing or hiding HUD elements does not touch them.

This is presentation, not state. Nothing is replicated, nobody else sees it, and none of it makes a player drunk or hurt: whatever decides that -- usually the server -- keeps it, and a client script asks for the picture to match. Weather and time of day are shared world state and are not touched.

Effects from every resource combine rather than overwrite each other, on top of the game's own grade -- which already desaturates the screen as health runs low -- rather than in its place: brightness, contrast and saturation multiply, the colour cast and the hue shift add, and blur, ghosting and blood each draw the strongest one asked for. The result does not depend on which resource asked first, and removing one effect leaves the game's grade and every other effect as they were.

An effect belongs to the resource that created it: only that resource can change or remove it, and it goes when the resource stops, when the session ends or when the level changes. A cinematic that resets the game's post-processing clears the screen until the effect next changes. Up to 64 effects are kept across every resource.

parameters.name: effect
parameters.description: Which effect, as `screenEffects` names it.

parameters.name: params
parameters.description: Values for the effect's own parameters, each clamped into its range. A parameter left out takes its default; one the effect does not take is an error.

type.name: { saturation?: number; brightness?: number; contrast?: number; cyan?: number; magenta?: number; yellow?: number; darkness?: number; hue?: number; amount?: number }

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: `fadeInMs` brings it up from nothing; `fadeOutMs` is how long it takes to go, when its duration runs out or when `removeScreenEffect` is called without a fade of its own; `durationMs` ends it on its own after that long, before its fade-out -- 0, the default, keeps it until it is removed. Fades are up to a minute.

type.name: { fadeInMs?: number; fadeOutMs?: number; durationMs?: number }

returns.description: A handle for `updateScreenEffect`, `removeScreenEffect` and `isScreenEffectActive`, or 0 when 64 effects are already on screen.

functions.name: updateScreenEffect
functions.description: Changes an effect while it is on screen -- a drunkenness that deepens with every drink, a wound that worsens.

parameters.name: handle
parameters.description: What `addScreenEffect` returned.

parameters.name: params
parameters.description: New values for some of the effect's parameters. The others keep theirs.

type.name: { saturation?: number; brightness?: number; contrast?: number; cyan?: number; magenta?: number; yellow?: number; darkness?: number; hue?: number; amount?: number }

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: `fadeMs` moves the parameters to their new values over that long, from wherever they are now; 0, the default, moves them at once.

returns.description: False when the handle is gone or belongs to another resource.

functions.name: removeScreenEffect
functions.description: Takes an effect off the screen. An effect already fading out carries on from where it is.

parameters.name: handle
parameters.description: What `addScreenEffect` returned.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: How long it takes to fade out. Left out, it fades over the `fadeOutMs` it was created with; 0 takes it off at once.

returns.description: False when the handle is gone or belongs to another resource.

symbols.name: Audio
symbols.description: The game's own sound triggers, played at this machine. A trigger is a name the game's audio data declares -- `a_o_bell_kkut_kostelni`, `c_torch_whoosh1`, `f_ge_cough_woman` -- standing for an FMOD event. The full vocabulary is `Libs/GameAudio/*.xml` in `IPL_GameData.pak`, with the gameplay-facing subset listed in `Libs/Tables/GameAudio/SkaldAtlTrigger.xml`. Nothing here is replicated: a sound everyone should hear is one the server tells every client to play. Every call returns false while the audio system is not up, which is the case before a world is loaded, and for a trigger name the audio data does not declare.

functions.name: play
functions.description: Plays a trigger with no position: heard at full volume wherever the player is, like a UI cue. It goes on the one global audio object every 2D sound in the game shares, which is why it cannot be stopped again.

parameters.name: trigger
parameters.description: Name of the trigger, spelled as the game's audio data spells it. Not text and not translated.

returns.description: True when the audio system took it.

functions.name: playAt
functions.description: Plays a trigger once at a point in the world, positioned and attenuated against the player's ears. The sound is handed to the engine and forgotten: it stays where it was put, plays to its end, and cannot be stopped or moved. Occlusion is ignored rather than ray-traced, so a wall between the point and the player does not silence it.

parameters.name: trigger
parameters.description: Name of the trigger, spelled as the game's audio data spells it.

parameters.name: position
parameters.description: Where to play it, in world-space metres.

returns.description: True when the audio system took it.

parameters.name: entityId

Clips play through the server's `playAnimation("", { clip })`.

symbols.name: Vfx
symbols.description: The game's own particle effects, played on this machine. An effect is a name out of the game's particle libraries -- `WH_Particels.fires.candle`, `collisions.combat.sword_sword`, `cinematics.dust.dust_army_a` -- and `list` is the whole vocabulary. Nothing here is replicated: an effect everyone should see is one the server tells every client to play with `Vfx.burst`, or one the server places with `Vfx.spawn`, which the interest grid then streams to whoever is near it. Almost every effect the game ships is continuous, which means it never ends on its own -- so everything started here is given a duration, and one that is not stopped first is stopped when the session ends.

functions.name: spawn
functions.description: Plays an effect standing at a point in the world, on an entity this client owns and removes again. Every spawn parameter is read once, when the emitter is created, so none of them can be changed afterwards -- stop it and start another.

parameters.name: effect
parameters.description: Name of the effect, spelled as the game's particle libraries spell it.

parameters.name: position
parameters.description: Where to play it, in world-space metres.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: `rotation` aims the emitter; `scale`, `countScale`, `speedScale` and `timeScale` multiply what the effect authored; `strength` feeds its strength curves; `pulsePeriod` restarts it on that many seconds; `prime` starts it already running, which is what a fire wants. `durationMs` is how long it lives -- two seconds by default, and an hour at most.

type.name: { rotation?: Quaternion | Vector3; scale?: number; countScale?: number; speedScale?: number; timeScale?: number; strength?: number; pulsePeriod?: number; prime?: boolean; durationMs?: number }

returns.description: A handle to pass to `stop`, or 0 when the world was not up, the budget was full or the game would not load the effect.

functions.name: attach
functions.description: Plays an effect in a free render slot of an entity, where it follows that entity: smoke off a cart, a glow around a body, dust under a horse. The slot is freed when the duration runs out, when `stop` is called, or when the entity goes. The offset is measured from the entity's own origin, not from a bone, so an effect cannot be pinned to a hand or a weapon this way.

parameters.name: effect
parameters.description: Name of the effect, spelled as the game's particle libraries spell it.

parameters.name: entityId
parameters.description: Engine entity to hang it on -- what `Player.entityId` reports. Entity ids are reused, so one is only meaningful while the entity is alive.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: As `spawn`, plus `offset`: where the emitter sits in the entity's own space, in metres. Up to 8 m from its origin.

type.name: { offset?: Vector3; rotation?: Quaternion | Vector3; scale?: number; countScale?: number; speedScale?: number; timeScale?: number; strength?: number; pulsePeriod?: number; prime?: boolean; durationMs?: number }

returns.description: A handle to pass to `stop`, or 0 when the entity was not there or the game would not load the effect.

functions.name: stop
functions.description: Stops one effect and releases what it was standing on.

parameters.name: handle
parameters.description: What `spawn` or `attach` returned.

returns.description: True when the handle named an effect that was still playing.

functions.name: stopAll
functions.description: Stops every effect this client started, including ones other resources started. The session ending does this too.

returns.description: Nothing.

functions.name: isPlaying
functions.description: Whether the effect behind a handle is still running. False once its duration has run out, its entity has gone, or the level has changed under it.

parameters.name: handle
parameters.description: What `spawn` or `attach` returned.

returns.description: True while it is playing.

functions.name: has
functions.description: Asks the game whether it can resolve an effect by this name, without playing it. False while no world is loaded, and for a name the catalog knows but this install's particle libraries no longer declare, so a resource that ships names can fail early rather than silently.

parameters.name: effect
parameters.description: Name to look for.

returns.description: True when the name resolves here and now.

functions.name: list
functions.description: Every effect name the shipped game declares, in order. Mined from the particle libraries at build time, so it is the same list on the server.

parameters.name: prefix
parameters.description: Keep only the names starting with this, e.g. `WH_Particels.fires` or `collisions.combat`.

functions.description: How many effects this client is playing right now, across every resource. The budget is 192.

returns.description: The number of live effects.

functions.name: destroy
functions.description: Removes this client-local light. Safe to repeat.

functions.name: spawn
functions.description: Creates a client-local point light until destroyed, its creating resource stops or errors, or the session/world ends. Throws when the world is unavailable, native creation fails or the shared 192-light budget is full.

parameters.name: position
parameters.description: World-space position in metres.

type.name: Vector3 | { x: number; y: number; z: number }

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Defaults to warm orange, intensity 1, radius 5 and shadows off.

properties.description: Client-local service handle, distinct from server network entity identifiers.

symbols.name: Blip
symbols.description: A mark this client owns on the game's compass and map screen.

constructor.name: constructor
constructor.description: Creates a handle for a blip that already exists; use Blip.create() to make one.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: Identifier of an existing blip.

functions.name: toString
functions.description: Formats this blip handle for logging and debugging.

returns.description: The blip's id, its type and its position, or a note that it is gone.

functions.name: remove
functions.description: Takes this blip off the compass and the map screen and out of the registry.

returns.description: True when it was still there to remove.

functions.name: create
functions.description: Puts a mark on this client's compass and map screen and keeps it there, rebuilding it whenever the game drops it.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Where the blip goes, and optionally which icon to draw it with, what state to give it, what the map screen calls it, whether it shows on the compass and the map screen -- both, by default -- and whether the map legend's switch for its icon hides it, as by default. `type` is one of the game's own compass mark names -- `Checkpoint`, `QuestGiver`, `Shop`, `GeneralPoi` and the rest -- and defaults to `GeneralPoi`; an unknown one is rejected rather than guessed at.

type.name: { position: Vector3; type?: string; state?: number; label?: string; compass?: boolean; map?: boolean; legend?: boolean }

returns.description: The new blip, or null at the blip limit.

functions.name: getById
functions.description: Looks a blip up by its id.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: Blip identifier.

returns.description: The blip's handle, or null when it no longer exists.

functions.name: all
functions.description: Lists every blip this client's scripts made. Blips the server placed are not included.

returns.description: One handle per live blip, in creation order.

functions.name: removeAll
functions.description: Takes every blip this client's scripts made off the compass and the map screen, leaving the server's blips and the game's own marks alone.

properties.name: id
properties.description: Identifier of this blip, unique for the lifetime of the session. Ids are not reused.

properties.name: valid
properties.description: Whether the blip is still in the registry. A handle to a removed blip keeps reading, and every other property reads as its default.

properties.name: live
properties.description: Whether the compass currently carries a mark for this blip. It goes false on its own whenever the game empties the compass -- a level load does -- and back to true on the next tick.

properties.name: position
properties.description: World-space position in metres. The compass recomputes bearing and distance from it every frame, so assigning moves the mark with no rebuild.

properties.name: type
properties.description: Which of the game's own compass icons the mark draws as, by the game's own name for it. Assignment rebuilds the native mark, because the icon is read once when a mark is registered and never re-read.

properties.name: state
properties.description: The mark's state, forwarded to the compass movie as-is. What a given value draws is undocumented; 0 is what a fresh mark carries.

properties.name: label
properties.description: The blip's name on the map screen, shown verbatim in place of the name the game gives its icon type; empty keeps that name. A compass mark has no text, so the compass never shows it.

properties.name: compass
properties.description: Whether the blip is drawn on the HUD compass. True by default.

properties.name: map
properties.description: Whether the blip is drawn on the map screen. True by default, but only for an icon the map has art for: `Main`, `Side`, `Micro`, `Checkpoint`, `Dlcs`, `Bailiff`, `FistFight` and `Racing` have none and stay on the compass. The map legend's switch for the blip's icon type hides it like one of the game's own unless `legend` is false, and a change to a blip on the open map is redrawn within a frame.

properties.name: legend
properties.description: Whether the map legend's switch for the blip's icon type hides it, as it does the game's own marks of that type. True by default. False keeps it on the map screen whatever that switch says, so a script can hide the game's own marks of a type with `WorldMap.setCategoryVisible` and still draw its own with the same icon.

symbols.name: DoorUse
symbols.description: The door a player's use is about, as this machine sees it when they use it.

properties.name: id
properties.description: The server's door entity, as server-side `door.id`; 0 when the server has not sent this door yet.

properties.name: guid
properties.description: The door's EntityGuid, as sixteen lowercase hex digits: the same value as server-side `door.guid`.

properties.name: name
properties.description: The entity name the level gives the door.

properties.name: open
properties.description: Whether the door stands open on this machine.

properties.name: locked
properties.description: Whether the door is locked on this machine.

symbols.name: LocationId
symbols.description: Native location or POI GUID fields.

properties.name: data1
properties.description: First GUID field, an unsigned 32-bit integer.

properties.name: data2
properties.description: Second GUID field, an unsigned 16-bit integer.

properties.name: data3
properties.description: Third GUID field, an unsigned 16-bit integer.

properties.name: data4
properties.description: The final eight GUID bytes, in native order.

symbols.name: WorldRayHit
symbols.description: One thing a trace met, as the machine that traced it saw it.

properties.name: position
properties.description: Where the ray met it, in world-space metres.

properties.name: normal
properties.description: The surface normal at that point, as a unit vector.

properties.name: distance
properties.description: How far along the ray it sits, in metres.

properties.name: surface
properties.description: The surface type's own name, spelled the way the game's tables spell it in `Libs/MaterialEffects/SurfaceTypes.xml` -- `mat_wood`, `mat_rock`, `mat_soil`, `mat_water`. It says what the thing is made of, which is how footsteps and blows sound, not what it is: a plank wall is `mat_wood` as much as a trunk is, so tell a tree by `category`. Among the 74 the game defines: `mat_wood`, `mat_wood_soft`, `mat_vegetation`, `mat_bushes`, `mat_rock`, `mat_rock_unwalk`, `mat_rock_horse_ignore`, `mat_stairs_stone`, `mat_gravel`, `mat_soil`, `mat_mud`, `mat_grass`, `mat_road`, `mat_metal`, `mat_glass`, `mat_plaster`, `mat_thatch`, `mat_fabric`, `mat_flesh`. Empty only before the material tables are up.

properties.name: terrain
properties.description: Whether the ground itself was hit rather than anything placed on it. Nothing lies behind the terrain, so a trace stops there. The same as `kind` being `terrain`.

properties.name: kind
properties.description: What sort of thing the ray stopped on. `entity` is anything with an `entityClass` -- doors, props, NPCs, players. `vegetation` is an instance the level paints on: trees, bushes, plants, and boulders painted the same way. `brush` is a static mesh placed one by one: walls, houses, rocks and cliffs. `static` is static geometry that is neither, or whose source the engine does not record. Trees and rocks are not entities, so for them this, `model` and `category` are what say what was hit.

properties.name: model
properties.description: The mesh of a vegetation instance or a brush, as the path the game loads it from -- `objects/natural/vegetation/trees/normal_trees/quercus_robur/quercus_robur_big_a.cgf`. Null for terrain, entities and `static`. A tree or a rock has no GUID, but its `model` and `position` together are the same on every client on the same level, which is what a server keeps a felled tree or a mined rock by.

properties.name: category
properties.description: Which of the game's own folders of natural objects `model` comes from: `tree` for `objects/natural/vegetation/trees` -- living, dead, fallen and stumps alike, which `model` tells apart -- `bush` for its bushes, `plant` for the rest of its vegetation (grass, ferns, mushrooms, branches), and `rock` for `objects/natural/rocks` and `objects/natural/stones`. Null for anything else, man-made included.

properties.name: material
properties.description: The material drawn where the ray met it, as the path the material manager keys it by, the sub-material when the mesh has several -- a trunk's bark rather than the tree's whole material. Null for terrain and when nothing names one.

properties.name: entityGuid
properties.description: The level's own identity for what was hit, as sixteen lowercase hex digits -- the same on every machine, and what `Door.find` and the other GUID lookups take. Null for terrain, for static geometry and for anything the session spawned, none of which the level names.

properties.name: entityName
properties.description: The name the level gives it, often empty. Null when nothing that carries a name was hit.

properties.name: entityClass
properties.description: The engine class it belongs to -- `AnimDoor`, `NPC_NAI`, `GeomEntity`. Null when nothing that carries a class was hit.

properties.name: entityId
properties.description: This machine's own handle for it. Local to this client and to this session -- it is not the network ID and it is not portable, so store `entityGuid` instead. Null for terrain and static geometry.

properties.name: levelObject
properties.description: The object the level placed that was hit, named the way `LevelEdit.apply` finds it again on every machine, with where the level put it and how it turned and sized it. A tree, a rock or a wall is one; so is a door or any other entity the level gives a GUID. Null for terrain, for static geometry the engine records no source for, and for anything the session spawned -- props, players, NPCs. Spread it into a definition to take the object out or swap it: `LevelEdit.apply({ ...hit.levelObject, model: stump })`.

properties.name: player
properties.description: The player whose body it was -- the local player's own included, when `ignoreSelf` is off -- or null for anything else. Found through the body's own entity, so it holds for a disguised player too: their collider is the mesh's size, and a trace that meets the mesh names them.

symbols.name: WorldLevelObject
symbols.description: An object the level placed, as a level edit keys it, and the pose the level gave it. Every field a `LevelEditDefinition` needs to find it again.

properties.name: kind
properties.description: A `brush` is a static mesh or a vegetation instance -- a wall, a rock, a tree -- found by its mesh and where the level put it. An `entity` is found by its GUID.

properties.name: name
properties.description: A brush's mesh path, the same as the hit's `model`; an entity's name.

properties.name: guid
properties.description: An entity's level GUID as sixteen lowercase hex digits; absent for a brush.

properties.name: class
properties.description: An entity's engine class; absent for a brush.

properties.name: at
properties.description: Where the level put it: its pivot, not the point the ray met. Unchanged while an edit has moved it, since it is the key.

properties.name: rotation
properties.description: How the level turned it, for a prop or effect standing in its place. `LevelEdit.apply` reads a rotation only with a `position`, so spreading this into a definition moves nothing.

properties.name: scale
properties.description: How the level sized it, per axis. Read only with a `position`, as `rotation` is.

symbols.name: WorldNearbyEntity
symbols.description: One entity a sphere reported, and where it stood when it did.

properties.name: position
properties.description: Where it is, in world-space metres.

properties.name: distance
properties.description: How far it is from the centre of the sphere, in metres.

properties.name: guid
properties.description: The level's own identity for it, as sixteen lowercase hex digits. Null for anything the session spawned, which the level does not name.

properties.name: name
properties.description: The name the level gives it, often empty.

properties.name: class
properties.description: The engine class it belongs to -- `AnimDoor`, `NPC_NAI`, `GeomEntity`.

properties.name: physicalized
properties.description: Whether the engine has built physics for it, which is what makes it something a trace could also find.

properties.name: entityId
properties.description: This machine's own handle for it. Local to this client and to this session -- it is not the network ID and it is not portable, so store `guid` instead.

symbols.name: World
symbols.description:
What this machine's engine can be asked about the level around it: what a trace meets, what the ground is under a point, and which entities are inside a sphere.

Each is the engine's own query rather than a search over everything loaded, so the cost is what the question covers. They answer inside the call, because this is the machine that has the world -- the server's `World` asks the same three questions as promises, because it has to borrow a client's world to answer them.

None of it is replicated and none of it is authority: an answer describes what one client has streamed in at one moment. A zone that matters is decided on the server, from an answer the server asked for itself.

functions.name: raycast
functions.description: Traces a segment through the world and reports the first thing it meets.

parameters.name: from
parameters.description: Where the ray starts, in world-space metres.

parameters.name: to
parameters.description: Where it ends. Up to 4096 metres away; a ray of no length is refused.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description:
`mode` picks which of the game's own three traces to run: `cover` asks whether the world is in the way -- static geometry, props and doors block, and bodies cannot, which is what a line of sight wants; `anything` asks what is under the ray, bodies included, which is what a pick wants; `ground` sees only surfaces a player could stand on. It defaults to `cover`, and a name that is none of the three is rejected rather than guessed at.

`ignoreSelf` passes the local player's own body through, and is on by default: the player stands where the camera does, so a trace from the camera would otherwise mostly hit them. Both of a body's colliders are skipped, not just the entity's.

returns.description: What it hit, or null when the ray met nothing and when this machine has no world loaded.

functions.name: raycastAll
functions.description: Traces a segment and reports everything solid along it, nearest first. Each hit is found by re-tracing past the one before, so a window does not hide the wall it is set in.

parameters.name: from
parameters.description: Where the ray starts, in world-space metres.

parameters.name: to
parameters.description: Where it ends. Up to 4096 metres away; a ray of no length is refused.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: `mode` and `ignoreSelf` are as `World.raycast` documents them. `maxHits` is how many things along the ray to report, up to 8 and 8 by default.

returns.description: What the ray met, nearest first; empty when it met nothing and when this machine has no world loaded.

functions.name: getGroundZ
functions.description:
The height of the ground under a point.

A trace rather than a terrain height, so it stands on whatever is actually there -- a bridge, a floor, a castle roof -- and not on the heightmap underneath it.

parameters.name: position
parameters.description: The point to look under, in world-space metres. Its own z is where the probe is centred.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: How far above the point the probe starts and how far below it reaches, in metres. 5 and 200 by default -- the 5 above is what lets a point already slightly underground still resolve -- and up to 512 each.

returns.description: The world-space z of what is underfoot, or null when the probe reached nothing within its range.

functions.name: resolveGround
functions.description: The same probe as `getGroundZ`, with everything it found rather than only the height: the slope it landed on, and what the surface is made of.

parameters.name: position
parameters.description: The point to look under, in world-space metres.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: How far above the point the probe starts and how far below it reaches, in metres. 5 and 200 by default -- the 5 above is what lets a point already slightly underground still resolve -- and up to 512 each.

returns.description: What is underfoot, or null when the probe reached nothing.

functions.name: entitiesInRadius
functions.description:
Every entity the engine has inside a sphere, nearest first.

This reads the engine's own spatial grid, so it costs what the sphere covers rather than what the level holds -- but it only sees what this client has streamed in, which for a distant point is nothing.

parameters.name: centre
parameters.description: The centre of the sphere, in world-space metres.

parameters.name: radius
parameters.description: Its radius in metres, up to 256.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: `class` reports only entities of that engine class -- `AnimDoor`, `NPC_NAI`, `GeomEntity` -- and a class the engine does not know matches nothing rather than everything; omitted, every class is reported. `max` is how many to report, nearest first, up to 64. `physicalOnly` skips entities the engine has built no physics for, which is the filter the game's own proximity query applies, and is off by default.

type.name: { class?: string; max?: number; physicalOnly?: boolean }

returns.description: The entities inside it, nearest first.

symbols.name: MapWaypoint
symbols.description: The marker the player has dropped on the map, as `WorldMap.getWaypoint` reports it.

properties.name: position
properties.description: Where the marker sits, in world-space metres. Its z is the terrain height under the point.

properties.name: mapId
properties.description: Which map it belongs to. The maps reuse one coordinate range.

symbols.name: WorldMap
symbols.description: The map screen at this machine, and the player's own marker on it. Nothing here is replicated: a marker everyone should see is one the server tells every client to make.

functions.name: getWaypoint
functions.description: Reads the marker the player has dropped on the map they are looking at. The game keeps at most one per map.

returns.description: The marker's position and the map it belongs to, or null when there is none.

functions.name: moveWaypoint
functions.description: Moves the marker the player has already dropped. It cannot create one, so it reads false when there is nothing down.

parameters.name: position
parameters.description: Where to put it, in world-space metres. Nothing snaps it to the terrain.

returns.description: True when there was a marker to move.

functions.name: clearWaypoint
functions.description: Takes the player's marker off the map they are looking at. It runs the game's own removal, so `mapWaypointCleared` is raised as it would be for the player.

returns.description: True when there was a marker to take off.

functions.name: isCategoryVisible
functions.description: Whether marks of this type are currently drawn on the compass and listed in the map legend.

parameters.name: type
parameters.description: One of the game's own compass mark types, spelled the way the game spells it -- `Shop`, `QuestGiver`, `GeneralPoi`. The full list is the `type` a `Blip` accepts.

returns.description: True when they are shown.

functions.name: setCategoryVisible
functions.description: Shows or hides a whole category of the game's own map markers -- every shop, every quest giver -- through the switch the map legend's rows drive. It affects the marks already placed as well as later ones. DLC icons share a legend row with the entry they belong to, so setting one sets the group.

parameters.name: type
parameters.description: One of the game's own compass mark types, spelled the way the game spells it -- `Shop`, `QuestGiver`, `GeneralPoi`. The full list is the `type` a `Blip` accepts.

parameters.name: visible
parameters.description: Whether marks of that type should be drawn.

returns.description: True when the map page was there to take it.

functions.name: discover
functions.description: Marks a place on this player's map as discovered, silently: no toast, no XP, no discovery trigger. What a resource that keeps a character's discoveries calls after the character is loaded, since every session starts on a fresh map. A point of interest raises `poiDiscovered` as it is marked; a location raises nothing.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: A point of interest or a location -- a town, a district -- as `poiDiscovered` or `locationDiscovered` handed it out. `data4` must be a Uint8Array of eight bytes.

returns.description: True when the id named a place in the loaded level; false otherwise, or before the level is up.

functions.name: revealFog
functions.description: Clears the fog of war around a point by the game's own reveal radius, as walking there does. What a resource that keeps where a character has been calls after the character is loaded. Only matters while the server's `reveal_map` is off; otherwise there is no fog.

parameters.name: position
parameters.description: A world-space point; only x and y count.

returns.description: True when the level's fog took it; false before the level is up.

functions.name: revealAllFog
functions.description: Clears the fog of war over the whole level, as the game's own `player_revealFow` does, and leaves discovery alone: places still become discovered when the player finds them. The fog is also what hides the names of places not yet found, so from then on the map writes a town's name only once the player knows of it. What a server that keeps `reveal_map` off for the discoveries, but wants no fog, calls once the character is loaded. A level load brings the fog back.

returns.description: True when the level's fog took it; false before the level is up.

properties.name: isOpen
properties.description: Whether the map screen is up right now. False in the main menu and across a level load, when there is no map page at all.

symbols.name: Compass
symbols.description: The compass strip along the top of the HUD, which is what this game has instead of a minimap. Marks go on it through `Blip`; this is the strip itself.

properties.name: markCount
properties.description: How many marks the compass carried at the last tick, the game's own included. Sampled rather than read live: the vector it comes from is reallocated by the thread that adds to it.

properties.name: visible
properties.description: Whether the compass is showing. Assignment pushes the game's own suppression, the one a cutscene uses, so it takes the whole strip rather than emptying it. It reads the mod's own view -- a suppression the game pushed is invisible here -- and the mod's is released when the session ends.

symbols.name: Travel
symbols.description: The local player's fast travel, as something to read. There is deliberately no verb: starting a travel moves the player, advances the world clock and can fire a random event, so in a session that is the server's decision rather than one for a resource on the traveller's own machine.

functions.name: canStart
functions.description: Asks the game whether a fast travel could begin right now, without starting one. The answer is the game's own refusal code; only 0 is proven, and it means yes.

returns.description: The refusal code, or null before the player module is up.

properties.name: active
properties.description: Whether a fast travel is running right now.

properties.name: position
properties.description: Where the travel has got to along its route, in world-space metres. Zero while none is running: check `active` first.

symbols.name: NoClipState
symbols.description: Where the free camera is and what it is doing.

properties.name: mode
properties.description: Whether the player's body is carried through the world or left behind.

properties.name: input
properties.description: Whether this machine's own keyboard and mouse are flying the camera.

properties.name: position
properties.description: Where the camera is, in world-space metres.

properties.name: forward
properties.description: The unit direction it is looking along.

properties.name: right
properties.description: The unit direction to its right, level with the horizon.

properties.name: up
properties.description: The unit direction out of the top of the frame.

properties.name: yaw
properties.description: Its heading in degrees, wrapped to -180..180. Zero faces +Y and a rising yaw swings left.

properties.name: pitch
properties.description: Its elevation in degrees, clamped to -89..89. Positive looks up.

properties.name: speed
properties.description: Metres a second at rest, before boost or crawl scales it.

properties.name: fov
properties.description: The vertical field of view in degrees the view was asked for.

properties.name: renderedFov
properties.description: The vertical field of view the renderer settled on, which `Hor+` adaptation and the window's aspect both move.

properties.name: aspectRatio
properties.description: Width over height, as the renderer reports it.

symbols.name: NoClip
symbols.description:
This machine's free camera, and what happens to the player's body while it is flying.

The view is a bodyless anchor entity made the active camera through the engine's own view system, so nothing is ever asked to sweep against the world. In `body` mode the player's entity is taken out of the physical world and placed at the camera each frame.

Client-only, and nothing here is an order another machine takes. It is not invisible to the session either: in `body` mode the thing being flown is the entity this client replicates, so the other players watch the flier go. In `camera` mode the body never moves.

The game's controls are held for as long as the flight lasts, whichever side is driving. The map editor (`MapEditor`) flies the same one camera: a flight in progress ends when the editor opens, and `enable` refuses while it is open.

functions.name: enable
functions.description: Starts flying. The camera begins where the player was looking, so this reads as stopping rather than as a cut.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description:
`mode` decides what happens to the player. `body`, the default, carries them: they pass through geometry, the world streams around them, the other players see them fly, and they land wherever the flight ends. `camera` leaves the body where it stands and touches nothing about its physics. A name that is neither is rejected rather than guessed at.

`input` is whether this machine's keyboard and mouse fly the camera -- on the keys the game's own photo mode is bound to in the controls menu (forward, back, left, right, jump to rise, crouch to sink, fast movement to boost), read through the active keyboard layout so AZERTY and the like work as the game does; Alt to crawl, mouse to turn. On by default; off, drive it with `move`.

`speed` is metres a second at rest, 0.05 to 400 and 12 by default. `fov` is the vertical field of view in degrees, up to 140; omitted, the view keeps the game's.

type.name: { mode?: "body" | "camera"; input?: boolean; speed?: number; fov?: number }

returns.description: `enabled` when the flight started. `alreadyActive` when one was already running -- the options are not re-applied. `noCamera` when there is no level to spawn the camera's anchor into. `cameraBusy` when the map editor holds the camera.

functions.name: disable
functions.description: Ends the flight, hands the view back and puts the body back into the physical world. Does nothing when no flight is running.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: `keepPosition` leaves the body where the camera stopped, and is the default. False puts it back where it took off from, facing the way it was. Neither means anything in `camera` mode.

returns.description: Nothing. `noclipChanged` reports the end with reason `script`.

functions.name: isActive
functions.description: Whether a flight is running at this machine.

returns.description: True while the free camera has the view.

functions.name: getState
functions.description: Everything about the flight in one read, rather than six calls that could each land on a different frame.

returns.description: The state, or null when no flight is running.

functions.name: getPosition
functions.description: Where the camera is, in world-space metres.

returns.description: Its position, or null when no flight is running.

functions.name: setPosition
functions.description: Puts the camera somewhere else without turning it.

parameters.name: position
parameters.description: Where to put it, in world-space metres. A non-finite position is ignored.

returns.description: True when the camera took the position; false when no flight is running.

functions.name: getRotation
functions.description: How the camera is aimed, in degrees. Two angles rather than a quaternion: that is what flying with a mouse produces, and it keeps the horizon level for free.

returns.description: Its angles, or null when no flight is running.

functions.name: setRotation
functions.description: Aims the camera without moving it.

parameters.name: rotation
parameters.description: The angles to take, in degrees. Either may be left out to keep the one the camera has. Yaw wraps to -180..180 and pitch is clamped to -89..89.

returns.description: True when the camera took the angles; false when no flight is running.

functions.name: getForward
functions.description: The unit direction the camera is looking along.

returns.description: Its view direction, or null when no flight is running.

functions.name: setPose
functions.description: Places and aims the camera in one go.

parameters.name: position
parameters.description: Where to put the camera, in world-space metres.

parameters.name: forward
parameters.description: The direction to aim it along. Need not be normalized; a direction of no length is ignored.

returns.description: True when the camera took the pose; false when no flight is running.

symbols.name: Camera
symbols.description:
The view this client is drawing through. Nothing here is replicated and nothing here is authority: it describes one machine's own camera at one moment.

This is the game's camera, not a camera of the mod's own -- it follows the player, a dialogue, a cutscene or a free flight, whichever the game currently has. `NoClip` is what takes it over, `setThirdPerson` puts it behind the player, and `setShot` stands it somewhere in the world.

functions.name: getPose
functions.description: Where the camera is this frame, and what it can see from there.

returns.description: The pose, or null in the main menu and across a level load, when there is no active view at all.

functions.name: screenRay
functions.description: A ray out of the camera through a point on screen. This is what turns "what is the player looking at" into the two points `World.raycast` takes.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: `x` and `y` are a point on screen in normalized device coordinates -- both run -1 at the left and bottom to +1 at the right and top, so the default (0, 0) is the centre of the screen, which is where the crosshair is. `range` is how far out to carry `target`, in metres, 100 by default and up to 4096.

type.name: { x?: number; y?: number; range?: number }

returns.description: The ray, or null when there is no active view.

functions.name: setThirdPerson
functions.description:
Puts this player's camera behind them, for as long as it is on.

The game has no third-person view to switch to, so this is a camera of the mod's own, placed every frame behind the body along the direction the player is looking. Nothing about their controls changes: they walk and turn as they did, and the mouse still turns the body. When a wall is behind them the camera comes in along the same line rather than going through it. Their head, which the game keeps out of its own first person, is drawn for as long as this camera is the one looking at them.

This is what a disguised player needs -- `player.setDisguise` hides the body the game's own camera sits in. It is this client's own view, so a gamemode turns it on from a client script, typically on an event the server sends the disguised player.

There is one view to draw through: `NoClip` cannot start while this holds it, and while `NoClip` flies this waits. The map, the inventory and the other pause-screen pages are filmed by the game's own camera, so this steps aside while one is open and comes back when it closes. It lasts until the session ends.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Where the camera sits, in metres: `distance` back from the body along where the player looks (3.5 by default, 0.3 to 20), `height` of the point it orbits above the body's feet (1.6, up to 5 either way), and `shoulder` to the right of it, negative for the left (0, up to 3 either way). Null hands the view back to the game's own camera. Called again while on, it only moves the camera.

type.name: { distance?: number; height?: number; shoulder?: number } | null

functions.name: isThirdPerson
functions.description: Whether `setThirdPerson` is on.

returns.description: True from `setThirdPerson` until it is turned off, also while it waits for a body or for `NoClip`.

functions.name: setShot
functions.description:
Films this player's view from a fixed point: what a cutscene, an intro or a kill cam is made of.

The camera holds there until `clearShot` -- or until another `setShot`, which glides on from wherever this one is. Nothing about the player's controls changes; a gamemode that wants them still says so through `Controls`. The player's head, which the game keeps out of its first person, is drawn for as long as the camera is looking at them from outside their eyes.

There is one view to draw through. A shot outranks `setThirdPerson`, which takes over again when the shot ends, and `NoClip` cannot start while it holds. The map, the inventory and the other pause-screen pages are filmed by the game's own camera, so the shot steps aside while one is open and comes back when it closes. A shot ends with the session.

The server can send the same shot with its own `Camera.setShot(player, options)`; whichever comes last wins.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: `position` is where the camera stands and `lookAt` the point it faces, both in world space. `duration` is how long it takes to get there from wherever the view is now, in milliseconds: 0, the default, is a cut, and the most is 60000. `fov` is the vertical field of view in degrees, 20 to 120; leave it out to keep the player's own.

type.name: { position: Vector3; lookAt: Vector3; duration?: number; fov?: number }

returns.description: True, or false while `NoClip` is flying or when `position` and `lookAt` are the same point.

functions.name: clearShot
functions.description: Gives the player their own view back. Does nothing without a shot.

parameters.name: duration
parameters.description: How long the glide back into the player's eyes takes, in milliseconds: 0, the default, is a cut, and the most is 60000. The glide follows the player if they move meanwhile. With `setThirdPerson` on, it ends behind them instead and their head stays drawn.

functions.name: isShotActive
functions.description: Whether a shot holds the view.

returns.description: True from `setShot`, including its glide in, until `clearShot`; false already while gliding back.

functions.name: create
functions.description:
Puts a preview into the world: the game's own geometry, with no body, no collision and nothing replicated.

This is what a build preview, a placement outline or a menu turntable is made of. It is not a prop -- nobody else can see it, and it does not survive a level load.

parameters.description:
`model` is one mesh from the shared prop catalog; `models` is several, which is how a blueprint of more than one piece is previewed. `offsets` and `rotations` line up with `models` by index and place each piece inside the ghost's own frame, so the whole thing turns and scales as one. A path the catalog does not carry is refused, because it is a path the server could never be asked to spawn afterwards.

`position`, `rotation` and `scale` are where the ghost stands. `tint` washes it in a colour, with `a` below 1 making it translucent; omitted, every mesh keeps the materials it shipped with.

type.name: { model?: string; models?: string[]; offsets?: Vector3[]; rotations?: Quaternion[]; position: Vector3; rotation?: Quaternion; scale?: number; tint?: Color }

returns.description: The ghost, or null when this client has no world, at the ghost limit, and when not one of the meshes would load.

symbols.name: PropPlacer
symbols.description:
Placement mode: a translucent preview under the crosshair, tinted for whether the spot is accepted, put down with a click.

The loop is native and runs with the game's own frame, so the preview tracks the camera exactly and no script runs per frame. While a session is up this client's input belongs to it, the way one of the game's own screens takes it -- which is what stops a confirm click also swinging the player's sword, and what stops the player walking away mid-placement.

One session at a time, and it belongs to the resource that started it: a resource that stops takes its session with it.

**Nothing here is authority.** The rules below colour a preview at one client. What actually gets built is the server's decision, made again from the pose the client confirmed -- two players aiming at the same patch of ground both see green.

functions.name: begin
functions.description: Starts placement. The preview appears under the crosshair on the same frame.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description:
`model`, `models`, `offsets` and `rotations` describe the preview exactly as `PropGhost.create` takes them.

`validTint` and `invalidTint` are the two colours the preview flips between, translucent green and translucent red by default. `range` is how far the aim ray reaches in metres (40 by default, up to 512) and `fallbackDistance` is where the preview sits when the ray reaches nothing. `verticalOffset` lifts or sinks it, `yaw` is a fixed turn added to whatever the aim settles on, and the mouse wheel moves that while a session is up.

`alignToSurface` stands the preview on the slope it is aimed at instead of upright; `faceAwayFromPlayer` turns it to face away from where you stand, which is what a wall or a tower wants and is on by default. `keepOpen` leaves the session running after a confirm so several can be placed in one go, and is on by default.

`rules` is what the preview is tinted by, and every one of them is off unless named. `maxSlope` is degrees the ground may lean; `surfaces` is which surface names are allowed; `minDistance` and `maxDistance` bound how far from the player it may stand; `clearance` is metres that must be free of other entities, narrowed to `clearanceClasses` when given; `requireSurface` refuses a spot the ray never reached, and is on by default.

type.name: { model?: string; models?: string[]; offsets?: Vector3[]; rotations?: Quaternion[]; scale?: number; validTint?: Color; invalidTint?: Color; range?: number; fallbackDistance?: number; verticalOffset?: number; yaw?: number; alignToSurface?: boolean; faceAwayFromPlayer?: boolean; keepOpen?: boolean; rules?: { maxSlope?: number; surfaces?: string[]; minDistance?: number; maxDistance?: number; clearance?: number; clearanceClasses?: string[]; requireSurface?: boolean } }

returns.description: True when the session started; false when one is already running, when this client has no world or camera, when another part of the mod holds the controls, and when the preview could not be built.

functions.name: end
functions.description: Ends the session and gives the player their input back. `end` is raised. Doing nothing when no session is running is not an error.

functions.name: isActive
functions.description: Whether a placement session is running at this client right now.

returns.description: True while one is up.

functions.name: setVeto
functions.description: Refuses every spot until cleared, which is where a rule the engine cannot answer belongs -- what the player can afford, what the server has already said no to. It latches, so it costs the placement loop nothing.

parameters.name: vetoed
parameters.description: Whether to refuse the spot whatever the rules say.

returns.description: True while a session is running.

functions.name: rotate
functions.description: Turns the preview, the same way the mouse wheel does while a session is up.

parameters.name: degrees
parameters.description: How far to turn it, in degrees. Negative turns the other way.

returns.description: True while a session is running.

functions.name: getPose
functions.description: Where the placement is aimed right now, without waiting for a `move`.

returns.description: The pose, or null when no session is running and before the first aim settles.

functions.name: on
functions.description: Listens for one of the session's events. Handlers belong to the resource that registered them and go when it stops.

parameters.name: event
parameters.description: `move` fires when the aim has travelled far enough to be worth reporting, and whenever the spot flips between accepted and refused -- it is throttled on purpose, because it is the one event that could otherwise fire every frame. `confirm` is a click the rules accepted, and is the one to send to the server. `rejected` is a click they refused, so the resource can say why; the session stays up. `cancel` is the player backing out. `end` is the session stopping, however it stopped, and is always the last one.

parameters.name: handler
parameters.description: Called with where the placement is aimed and whether that spot is accepted. The pose is null for `cancel` and `end`.

returns.description: A function that removes this subscription.

symbols.name: ActionHint
symbols.description:
"Press [key] to ..." hints, drawn by the game's own HUD beside its own, with a handler run when the player presses the key.

A hint names one of the game's keys by its control -- `primary_action`, `jump` and the rest of `keys()` -- and never a physical key: the glyph is whatever the player has bound to that control, keyboard or pad, and follows a rebind. A press hint fires on the press; a hold hint draws the game's ring and fires once it fills.

Hints are drawn while the player is in control of their character, on foot or in the saddle, and the game takes them down in dialogue, minigames and menus. Two hints on one key stack: the newest is drawn and gets the press, and removing it brings back the one under it. A hint normally leaves the game's own action on that key enabled. `chat_focus_follow_init` replaces the native focus/follow toggle while its hint is shown, so a scripted Follow action receives one press.
